summary: The first in a planned series of surveys by Charles Kline at UCLA asking ARPANET sites how they had implemented host-to-host protocol. This one covers Network Control Programs, the software that handled network connections, and asks for a reply within two weeks. Later surveys were to cover Telnet and RJE.

plainLanguage.summary: A questionnaire asking each computer site to describe the program that handles its network connections, so the answers could be collected and shared.

questions: what is a network control program
subtitle: UCLA's questionnaire asking ARPANET sites how they built their Network Control Programs.

tldr.problem: There was no collected information on how different sites had implemented the host to host protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Charles Kline of UCLA describes what he means by an NCP and poses numbered questions on hardware, coding, sizes, buffers, timeouts and protocol features.
tldr.outcome: Replies were requested within two weeks and the results were to be published. It is the first in a series, and later ones were to cover Telnet and RJE.

today: RFC 460 has no recorded status and is a one-time questionnaire, so it is a historical record rather than a specification. RFC 459 is a complaint about it.

sections.title: Purpose of the Survey
sections.content:
RFC 460, from Charles Kline at UCLA, is the first in a series requesting information on how the host to host protocol was implemented. Sites are asked to reply within two weeks, for example by copying the RFC at the NIC and inserting answers. The results will be published.

This one covers Network Control Programs (NCPs). Future RFCs are to deal with Telnet, RJE and so on.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a form to fill in about how your computer talks on the network, with more forms to come.

sections.title: What the Author Means by an NCP
sections.content:
An NCP is the part of the system that performs the tasks needed for host to host protocol as specified in document NIC 7104 (the protocols notebook). The survey says an NCP has four parts, though not necessarily as separate pieces:

  • code for connection establishment, including the rendezvous table of open and pending connections;
  • code for transmission over open connections, including buffer management and sending allocate and giveback commands;
  • code that moves messages in and out of the Imp, sometimes called the Imp handler;
  • other code such as measurements and initialization.
sections.plainLanguage: The NCP is the helper program that sets up and looks after connections between computers.

sections.title: The Questions
sections.content:
The questions cover general information (host name, main cpu, operating system, documentation), the Imp interface, and how the NCP was coded and maintained, including man-months of effort. They ask for the size of the code and tables, how the Imp handler works, how the NCP talks to user processes and which byte sizes are allowed.

Others ask about initial buffer allocation and when a giveback is sent, whether error commands are sent and logged, and whether connections are queued. The survey also asks about timeouts, measurements of the effect of network use, and any planned changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The form asks how big the program is, who wrote it, how it holds on to messages, and how long it waits before giving up.
